items.title: Direct multiple shooting
items.summary: The root question's scheme verbatim: guess the trajectory at every grid point, integrate each sub-interval from its guessed value in parallel, then force continuity with a Newton iteration (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_multiple_shooting_method).
items.root_link: Bears on Q1, whether a single long sequential simulation can be parallelised over time by guessing the whole trajectory and Newton-correcting every step at once.
items.sequential: One answer is one trajectory needing k Newton iterations, each a forward substitution in which interval t's correction waits on interval t-1 (O(m) deep for m intervals), while the m segment integrations are independent and parallelise exactly; the correction chain is the only serial residue because J is block lower-bidiagonal (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/parareal.pdf).

items.title: Parareal
items.summary: The cheap-Jacobian realisation of multiple shooting, introduced by Lions, Maday and Turinici: a coarse serial propagator predicts the trajectory and fine integrators correct each interval in parallel, iterating to convergence (https://parallel-in-time.org/methods/parareal.html).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2, whether the guess+Newton-correct trick only works when the system forgets its past, and on Q1.
items.sequential: Each iteration marches a coarse propagator serially over all T subintervals (step t waits on t-1) while the T fine integrations are independent, so one run's depth is k·T with k set by the forward decay of the coarse-guess error (the forgetting rate), which Gander and Hairer show is superlinear only for contractive systems (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/Preprints/gander_plenary2007.pdf).

items.title: MGRIT (XBraid)
items.summary: The non-intrusive multigrid-reduction-in-time version of Parareal (shipped as XBraid), which coarsens the time grid rather than using a separate coarse model (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
items.root_link: Bears on Q3, whether compute is a blocker and could be fixed with massive GPU parallelism.
items.compute_open: settled: for parabolic (dissipative) PDEs MGRIT is demonstrated to be an optimal-scaling solver, and LLNL reports 'tenfold or more' time-to-solution drops for compressible Navier-Stokes, so more parallel compute is already known to pay off there (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1184744; https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).
items.sequential: One run keeps the same coarse/fine structure as Parareal — a coarse-grid correction sweeps the time levels in order while fine-grid integrations are independent — and the iteration count is set by the contraction (forgetting) rate, not processor count, so the causal coarse sweep cannot be reordered without cyclic reduction (https://computing.llnl.gov/projects/parallel-time-integration-multigrid).

items.title: ParaDiag / ParaExp (linear diagonalisation)
items.summary: Direct time-parallel methods for linear dynamics: x_T = A^T x_0 is computed by diagonalisation or repeated squaring in O(log T) depth, giving exact parallel-in-time with no forgetting assumption (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2's exception, the one regime where the causality principle can be cleanly side-stepped, and on Q1.
items.sequential: none: the T sequential steps already collapse because the propagator A^T can be composed out of order by repeated squaring/diagonalisation in O(log T) parallel steps (https://www.unige.ch/~gander/siamtoc3.php).

items.title: Parallel cyclic reduction
items.summary: Parallel cyclic reduction solves the block-bidiagonal Newton correction (a tridiagonal/bidiagonal system) in O(log N) steps with N-fold parallelism, dropping the per-iteration depth of PinT methods from O(T) to O(log T) (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
items.root_link: Bears on Q3, the 'shit ton of GPU parallelism' question, specifically whether width can shorten the cheap sequential part.
items.compute_open: settled: N-fold parallel cyclic reduction is known to solve a tridiagonal system in O(log N) steps instead of O(N), so more parallel compute already buys the O(T)→O(log T) per-iteration depth reduction (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).
items.sequential: The block-bidiagonal solve is a forward substitution in which row t waits on row t-1 (O(T) deep per iteration), but the rows need not run in order: cyclic reduction eliminates independent pairs simultaneously, which pays off only when the T equations can be halved each round and the machine has ~T processors to feed them (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs554/fa2015/notes/09_tridiagonal_8up.pdf).

items.title: Speculative prefetching (MCMC)
items.summary: The MCMC analog of guess+correct: speculatively evaluate many possible accept/reject branches in parallel, keep the true path, discard the rest, with a speedup that is bounded and constant-factor (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2 for MCMC, whether the trick only works when the system forgets, and on Q3's width-versus-depth point.
items.sequential: One MH chain is a serial accept/reject sequence (each proposal waits on the previous accepted state, T steps per run), and prefetching speculates J future branches in parallel but keeps one path, giving O(log2 J) depth with J cores and expected speedup ≈1/α ≈ 4.3 at the 0.234 acceptance rate, largest when rejection dominates (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.7265).

items.title: Regeneration / splitting (MCMC)
items.summary: Splitting an MCMC sampler at regeneration times yields i.i.d. tours that can be simulated in parallel, avoiding the bias of many short independent chains (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2 for MCMC, where regeneration is the operational 'forgets its past' condition.
items.sequential: none: the tours between regeneration times are i.i.d. and already split into independent pieces that can run on separate processors, leaving only the mixing-governed length of one tour as the serial residue (https://galton.uchicago.edu/~mykland/paperlinks/MyklandTierneyYu2291148.pdf).

items.title: Coupling from the past (CFTP)
items.summary: Propp-Wilson exact sampling: run the chain from all possible states simultaneously under a monotone coupling, and coalescence certifies an exact draw, efficient only when coalescence (mixing) is fast (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2 for MCMC, where coalescence is the 'forgets its past' condition.
items.sequential: none: the coupled chains run from all states in parallel under one monotone update, so the work already splits across states, and the only serial quantity is the coalescence time, which is set by mixing, not compute (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/206-RWG/RWGpapers/propp_wilson.pdf).

items.title: Many-chain / data-parallel sampling (TFP HMC)
items.summary: GPUs/TPUs add width two ways — many chains at once and data-parallel gradient/log-density evaluation within one chain — but width does not shorten a single chain's critical path (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).
items.root_link: Bears on Q3, the GPU question, specifically the width-versus-depth distinction.
items.compute_open: The quantity more parallel compute would buy is the number of independent chains/seeds analysed: Angelino et al. show running many chains 'does not change the mixing time for any single chain' (https://lips.cs.princeton.edu/pdfs/angelino2014accelerating.pdf), and no cited source establishes whether adding more chains/seeds above that changes the posterior estimate (e.g. finds additional modes).
items.sequential: none: many chains and within-chain data-parallel likelihoods are already independent pieces, so the answer already splits across GPUs, and the per-chain critical path (T × per-step cost × mixing overhead) is unchanged by width (https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2022/11/13/stan-and-tensorflow-for-fast-parallel-bayesian-inference/).

items.title: GLUE / rainfall-runoff parameter calibration
items.summary: The actual compute burden in daily-step rainfall-runoff modelling is Monte-Carlo parameter calibration and GLUE uncertainty analysis, parallelised with MPI/OpenMP/CUDA across parameter sets, explicitly not across time steps (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).
items.root_link: Bears on Q3, the hydrology example showing compute is not a time-dimension blocker.
items.compute_open: settled: the compute burden is parameter calibration/GLUE uncertainty, parallelised across parameter sets (embarrassingly parallel, never across time), so more parallel compute is already known to buy parameter-set throughput, not time-step depth (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810; https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/12/10/2667).
items.sequential: none: each parameter set is one cheap forward run of a lumped model and parameter sets are independent, so the work already splits into independent pieces with no serial time chain to shorten (https://doi.org/10.3390/w15152810).

items.title: Chaotic / non-forgetting PinT
items.summary: On chaotic systems (Lorenz, hyperbolic PDEs) the coarse-guess error is amplified forward, so Parareal diverges or its superlinear convergence stops, because chaotic initial value problems are inherently ill-conditioned (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928; https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
items.root_link: Bears on Q2, whether the trick only works when the system forgets, here the non-forgetting failure mode.
items.compute_open: The quantity more parallel compute would buy is the coarse-grid resolution or number of processors fed to the coarse propagator: published results stop at divergence ('parareal diverging in many cases', https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880928), and whether scaling coarse-grid fidelity or iteration count changes convergence above that is unresolved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).
items.sequential: The coarse propagator must march the time levels in order (step t waits on t-1), so one run's depth is T × k iterations, and the positive-Lyapunov amplification means the iterations cannot be collapsed by reordering the causal chain; the nearest attempt at a fix is the coarse-grid-correction study in (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10441).

items.id: Measure the forgetting rate by feature-level causal tracing
items.title: Feature-level causal tracing turns the framer's forgetting condition into a measurement on the real system
items.summary: Perturb one SAE feature (or hidden state) at layer/token t and trace its indirect effect at t+s; the decay of that effect with lag is the empirical forgetting rate (Lyapunov exponent / mixing) the framer says decides whether guess-then-correct converges. It is the harry lens's 'start two runs a hair apart' done at feature resolution, and it does not itself restructure the computation.
items.root_link: It bears on the 'does that only work when the system forgets its past?' clause of the root question: it measures the forgetting rate in the actual system.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys more features, layers, and prompts analysed for the decay curve; published measurements stop at causal tracing of GPT-2 XL (1.5B, 48 layers) over 1,000 statements (https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262) and a 34M-feature SAE on one middle layer of Claude 3 Sonnet (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/); unknown above that is whether a full layer-to-layer feature-decay curve generalises to production-scale models across all layers and long contexts.
items.sequential: none: the clean, corrupted, and restored forward passes for each (layer, token, feature, statement) perturbation are independent, so the analysis already splits into one forward pass per perturbation with no step waiting on another, each keeping a GPU busy with a single model forward pass.

items.id: Linear feature representation -> parallel-in-time for free
items.title: SAE features give the linear basis that triggers the framer's no-forgetting parallel-in-time exception
items.summary: If the residual-stream trajectory is a linear combination of sparse features, the per-step feature transition is (approximately) linear and x_T = A^T x_0 is computable in O(log T) depth by repeated squaring / diagonalisation (the framer's ParaDiag exception), with no forgetting needed. Goodfire-style SAEs supply the linear decomposition; the open question is whether the feature-to-feature transition is stable enough to compose out of order.
items.root_link: It bears on the 'can a long sequential simulation be parallelised over time by guessing and correcting' clause: it is the one regime where the answer is yes without needing the system to forget.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys more models, layers, and features analysed to test feature-level linearity; published evidence stops at linear representations of concepts in LLaMA-2 7B (https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658) and SAE decompositions of up to 34M features on one middle layer of Claude 3 Sonnet (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/); unknown above that is whether the residual stream's feature-to-feature transition is linear and time-invariant across all layers and long contexts.
items.sequential: none: checking linearity is a per-feature regression/probe fit that is independent across features, layers, and models, so it already splits into parallel pieces with no step waiting on another.

items.id: Feature steering as the guess-then-correct operator
items.title: Feature steering is a learned correction operator that replaces the Newton step
items.summary: Instead of a Newton correction J^{-1}F, correct a guessed trajectory by clamping an SAE feature at an intermediate layer (add a constant in the direction of that feature) and continue the forward pass; a single feature edit (Golden Gate Claude) reliably propagates through the remainder of generation, and the [-5,5] steering sweet spot is the empirical analog of the framer's forgetting/contraction condition, outside which the correction destabilises downstream.
items.root_link: It bears on the 'correcting every step at once with Newton iterations' clause of the root question: it substitutes a learned, interpretable correction operator for the Newton solve.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys more features, steering strengths, and prompts swept; published measurements stop at 29 features across steering factors -20 to 20 on Claude 3 Sonnet (https://www.anthropic.com/research/evaluating-feature-steering) and Goodfire steering of Llama 3.3 70B at layer 50 (https://www.goodfire.com/research/mapping-latent-spaces-llama); unknown above that is whether a steering correction can be composed across many layers and tokens as a multiple-shooting operator without degrading capabilities.
items.sequential: none: once an SAE and a candidate feature are fixed, each steering evaluation is one independent forward pass that splits across features, strengths, and prompts; the only prerequisite is the embarrassingly parallel SAE training and attribution, not a per-answer chain.

items.id: Speculative and Jacobi decoding: the working guess-then-correct
items.title: Autoregressive decoding is the LLM instantiation of the framer's problem, and guess-then-correct already works there, gated by the forgetting interp measures
items.summary: Decoding K tokens is K serial forward passes, and the guess-whole-trajectory-then-correct solution is speculative decoding (draft several tokens ahead, verify in one parallel pass; 2-3x on T5-XXL, identical outputs) and Jacobi parallel decoding (initialise the whole sequence, refine all tokens in parallel to a fixed point; up to 38% speedup, ~2x on parallel resources). Both pay off exactly when the model forgets fast, i.e. the draft/target acceptance rate E[min(p,q)] is high, which is the quantity interp tools (tuned lens, causal tracing) measure.
items.root_link: It bears on the whole root question restated for the neural sequential computation: it is the concrete, shipped version of 'guess the whole trajectory and correct every step', whose success is the forgetting condition.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys more prompts and draft/target pairs analysed to measure the acceptance rate; published measurements stop at 2-3x speedup on T5-XXL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192) and up to 38% (nearly 2x on parallel resources) on translation models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10427); unknown above that is how the acceptance rate scales with model size, draft quality, and context length, and whether it stays high enough for near-linear parallel speedups on frontier models.
items.sequential: One decode still waits step-after-step: speculative decoding cuts the K-serial-token chain to roughly K/(gamma+1) rounds, each round drafting gamma tokens with a small model then verifying all gamma+1 candidate prefixes in one parallel pass of the target model (one run, the verify pass filling a GPU batch). The steps need not stay in order: Jacobi decoding initialises every token and refines them all in parallel each iteration, which pays off only if token dependencies are weak enough to reach a fixed point in few iterations, as tried by Santilli et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10427).
